courses.title: Dental Materials Science
courses.description: Properties of dental materials, restorative materials (amalgam, composites, glass ionomers), cements, impression materials, gypsum, alloys and ceramics.

topics.title: Properties of Dental Materials
topics.summary: Mechanical, thermal, chemical and biological properties relevant to dentistry.

material.heading: Mechanical properties
material.body: Stress is force per unit area; strain is deformation per unit length. The elastic modulus (Young's modulus — stress/strain in the elastic region) measures stiffness; enamel is stiff, dentine less so. The proportional and elastic limits mark the end of elastic behaviour; yield strength is the stress producing a specified permanent deformation. Ultimate strength is the maximum stress before fracture (compressive, tensile, flexural). Brittle materials (ceramics, amalgam, gypsum) are strong in compression but weak in tension; ductile materials (gold alloys) deform plastically. Toughness is energy absorbed before fracture; resilience is energy absorbed elastically. Hardness (Vickers, Knoop) relates to wear. Creep is time-dependent deformation under load (e.g. amalgam creep causing marginal breakdown). Fatigue failure occurs under repeated cyclic loading.
keyPoints: Brittle: strong in compression, weak in tension

material.heading: Thermal, chemical and biological
material.body: Coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) should match tooth structure to prevent microleakage — composites have higher CTE than tooth; glass ionomers are close to dentine. Thermal conductivity: metals (amalgam) conduct heat and may need a liner/base over deep cavities; composites and GIC are insulators. Wettability and contact angle affect adhesion and impression detail. Corrosion (electrochemical) and galvanism (different metals in contact producing current and pain) occur in the oral environment. Dimensional stability, setting reactions and water sorption also matter. Biocompatibility: materials should be non-toxic, non-irritant, non-allergenic (e.g. nickel allergy, latex, methacrylate sensitisation) and non-carcinogenic; tested by cytotoxicity, implantation and usage tests. ISO and ADA specifications set standards.
keyPoints: Metals conduct heat — use a base

topics.title: Dental Amalgam
topics.summary: Composition, setting reaction, properties, handling and mercury safety.

material.heading: Composition and setting
material.body: Dental amalgam is an alloy of mercury with a powder containing silver, tin and copper (plus sometimes zinc). The setting reaction in conventional (low-copper) amalgam: Ag3Sn (γ) + Hg → Ag2Hg3 (γ1, matrix) + Sn7-8Hg (γ2 — weakest, most corrosion-prone phase) + unreacted γ. High-copper amalgams (> 12% Cu, admixed or single-composition) eliminate the γ2 phase by forming Cu6Sn5 (η), improving strength, corrosion resistance and marginal integrity and reducing creep. Particle shapes: lathe-cut, spherical (requires less mercury and less condensation force) and admixed. Trituration (mixing in capsules with an amalgamator) and condensation (removing excess mercury, adapting to walls) are key handling steps; zinc-containing amalgam contaminated with moisture causes delayed expansion.

material.heading: Use and safety
material.body: Amalgam is durable, strong, cheap and technique-tolerant — suited to posterior load-bearing restorations — but is non-aesthetic, non-adhesive (needs mechanical retention and removal of sound tooth), and conducts heat. Mercury hygiene: use pre-capsulated amalgam, work in well-ventilated rooms, avoid skin contact, store scrap under fixer or water in sealed containers, use amalgam separators, clean up spills with a mercury spill kit (never a vacuum cleaner), and monitor mercury levels. The Minamata Convention on Mercury (Nigeria is a party) calls for a phase-down of amalgam use through caries prevention and alternatives; many countries restrict use in children under 15 and pregnant women. Placed amalgam restorations are not considered harmful to patients, and removal of intact amalgams is not recommended.

topics.title: Resin Composites and Adhesion
topics.summary: Composition, polymerisation shrinkage, light curing, and enamel/dentine bonding.

material.heading: Composites
material.body: Resin composites consist of an organic resin matrix (Bis-GMA, UDMA, diluted with TEGDMA), inorganic filler particles (silica, glass — increasing strength and reducing shrinkage), a silane coupling agent bonding filler to matrix, and an initiator system (camphorquinone — activated by blue light around 470 nm — with an amine accelerator). Classification by filler size: macrofilled, microfilled (polishable), hybrid/microhybrid and nanofilled (strength plus polish); flowable composites have less filler; bulk-fill composites cure in thicker increments (4–5 mm). Polymerisation shrinkage (about 2–3%) creates stress, marginal gaps and post-operative sensitivity — reduced by incremental placement (2 mm layers), low C-factor configurations and adequate curing. Oxygen inhibits polymerisation at the surface. Light-curing units (LED) must be checked for output with a radiometer.

material.heading: Adhesion
material.body: Enamel bonding (Buonocore, 1955): phosphoric acid etching (30–37%, about 15–30 seconds) creates micro-porosities; resin tags give reliable micromechanical retention. Dentine bonding is more challenging due to its water content, tubules and smear layer. Etch-and-rinse systems (3-step: etch, prime, bond; or 2-step) remove the smear layer; primer and adhesive infiltrate the demineralised collagen to form the hybrid layer (Nakabayashi). Self-etch systems use acidic monomers without rinsing, modifying the smear layer (less sensitivity; selective enamel etching improves enamel bonds). Universal adhesives work in either mode. Moisture control (rubber dam) is critical. Over-drying etched dentine collapses collagen, reducing bond strength (wet bonding technique).

topics.title: Glass Ionomers and Dental Cements
topics.summary: GIC chemistry and uses, resin-modified GIC, ART, and luting and lining cements.

material.heading: Glass ionomer cements
material.body: Glass ionomer cements (GICs) set by an acid–base reaction between fluoroaluminosilicate glass powder and polyacrylic acid (with tartaric acid controlling setting). Advantages: chemical adhesion to enamel and dentine (ionic bonding to calcium), fluoride release and recharge (caries-inhibiting), CTE similar to tooth and biocompatibility. Disadvantages: low fracture toughness and wear resistance, and sensitivity to moisture during early setting (protect with varnish or bonding agent). Resin-modified GICs (RMGIC) add HEMA and light-curing, improving strength and early moisture resistance. Uses: cervical (abrasion/erosion) lesions, primary teeth restorations, liners/bases, luting, fissure sealing and the Atraumatic Restorative Treatment (ART) — hand excavation of caries and restoration with high-viscosity GIC, without electricity or drills — WHO-endorsed and valuable in rural Nigerian communities and school programmes.

material.heading: Other cements
material.body: Zinc phosphate cement (zinc oxide + phosphoric acid) — traditional luting cement; initially acidic (pulpal irritation), exothermic (mix on a cool glass slab in small increments), no adhesion. Zinc oxide–eugenol (ZOE) — sedative/obtundent effect on the pulp, used for temporary restorations and root canal sealers; eugenol inhibits resin polymerisation, so avoid under composites. Calcium hydroxide (high pH ~12; antibacterial; stimulates reparative dentine) — liner for pulp capping; mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) and calcium silicate cements (e.g. Biodentine) now preferred for pulp capping, pulpotomy, perforation repair and apexification. Polycarboxylate cement adheres to tooth and is kind to the pulp. Resin cements are used for bonding ceramics and indirect composites.

topics.title: Impression Materials, Gypsum and Prosthetic Materials
topics.summary: Impression materials, dental stones, acrylic resins, alloys and ceramics.

material.heading: Impressions and gypsum
material.body: Impression materials: non-elastic (impression compound, zinc oxide–eugenol paste, impression plaster — for edentulous mouths) and elastic. Elastic hydrocolloids: alginate (irreversible; sets by reaction of sodium alginate with calcium sulfate, retarded by trisodium phosphate; cheap and widely used for study models and dentures; dimensionally unstable — syneresis and imbibition — so pour within about 10–15 minutes) and agar (reversible). Elastomers: polysulfide, condensation silicone (by-product causes shrinkage), addition silicone/polyvinyl siloxane (most accurate and stable; setting inhibited by latex gloves) and polyether (rigid, hydrophilic). Gypsum products (calcium sulfate hemihydrate + water → dihydrate): Type I impression plaster, Type II model plaster (β-hemihydrate, porous), Type III dental stone (α-hemihydrate), Type IV die stone (high strength, low expansion) and Type V (high strength, high expansion). Higher water/powder ratio weakens gypsum.

material.heading: Acrylics, alloys and ceramics
material.body: Denture bases are made of heat-cured polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA): powder (polymer beads with benzoyl peroxide initiator) and liquid (methyl methacrylate monomer with hydroquinone inhibitor). Proper curing cycles avoid porosity; residual monomer can irritate mucosa. Self-cured (cold-cure) acrylics are used for repairs and temporary crowns. Casting alloys: high-noble (gold), noble, and base metal (cobalt–chromium — for removable partial denture frameworks; nickel–chromium — metal-ceramic crowns, with nickel allergy concerns). Titanium is used for dental implants because of biocompatibility and osseointegration. Dental ceramics: feldspathic porcelain (aesthetic, brittle), glass-ceramics (lithium disilicate — strong and aesthetic), and polycrystalline zirconia (very strong; used for crowns, bridges and implant abutments). Metal-ceramic crowns bond porcelain to an oxide layer on the alloy. CAD/CAM milling and 3D printing are transforming fabrication.
